result.markdown: --- title: "Normal Distribution" author: "Mine Doğucu" filters: - quarto - a11y-tables.lua execute: echo: true format: revealjs: menu: openButton: false footer: | [stat-100.com](https://stat-100.com) code-line-numbers: false slide-number: true incremental: false theme: [default, style.scss] logo: path: images/00-stat100-logo-square.png alt: "STAT 100 course square logo" transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: "images/stat100-logo-rectangle.png" data-background-size: 10% data-background-position: 50% 85% data-aria-label: "STAT 100 course logo" --- ::: {.cell} ::: # Normal distribution {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"} ## A familiar shape ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Three histograms side by side. Left: heights of 260 physically active women, centered near 165 cm. Middle: heights of 247 physically active men, centered near 178 cm. Right: heights of 435 NBA players, centered near 201 cm. All three are roughly symmetric and bell shaped.' width=1344} ::: ::: Many variables have a symmetric, bell-shaped distribution. Data: [bdims](https://openintrostat.github.io/openintro/reference/bdims.html) and [nba_heights](https://openintrostat.github.io/openintro/reference/nba_heights.html) in the `openintro` package. ## Normal distribution The __normal distribution__ is a symmetric, bell-shaped curve. It is completely described by two numbers: - its __mean__: where the center is, - its __variance__, or __standard deviation__ (the square root of the variance): how spread out it is. . . . ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Histogram of the heights of active women with a smooth green normal curve on top. The curve, with mean 165 cm and standard deviation 6.5 cm, follows the shape of the histogram closely.' width=1056} ::: ::: Heights of active women are approximately normal with mean 165 cm and standard deviation 6.5 cm. ## Changing the mean ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Three normal curves with the same standard deviation, 6.5, centered at 150, 165, and 180. Changing the mean slides the curve left or right without changing its shape.' width=1056} ::: ::: . . . The mean moves the curve left and right. ## Changing the standard deviation ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Three normal curves all centered at 165 with standard deviations 4, 6.5, and 12. The curve with standard deviation 4 is tall and narrow; the one with 12 is short and wide.' width=1056} ::: ::: . . . The standard deviation makes the curve narrower or wider. The total area under the curve is always 1, so a narrower curve is taller. ## SAT scores From here on, we will use SAT scores as our example. We will assume that total SAT scores have - mean 1000 - standard deviation 200 and SAT Math scores have mean 500 and standard deviation 100. These values are close to, but not the same as, recent SAT scores: we altered them to make mental math easier. ::: {.cell} ::: ## Notation $$\text{random variable} \sim N(\text{mean}, \text{variance})$$ . . . ::: {.stat-callout .example} **Example** Let $X$ be the total SAT score of a randomly selected test taker. $$X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$$ is read "$X$ is normally distributed with mean 1000 and variance $200^2$." The standard deviation is 200 and the variance is $200^2 = 40{,}000$. ::: ## Many ways to say the same thing All of these mean the same thing: - $X$ is normally distributed with mean 1000 and variance 40,000. - $X$ is normally distributed with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. - $X \sim N(1000, 40{,}000)$ - $X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$ - $X \sim \text{Normal}(\text{mean} = 1000, \text{sd} = 200)$ ## Careful! ::: {.stat-callout .note-tip} **Note** Some books and some software put the standard deviation (not the variance) as the second number. In R, `pnorm()`, `qnorm()`, and `rnorm()` all use the standard deviation: `pnorm(1200, mean = 1000, sd = 200)` Always check whether the second number is the standard deviation or the variance. Writing it as $200^2$ makes it clear. ::: ## Reading the notation {.smaller} ::: {.stat-callout .exercise} **Exercise** For each normal distribution, find the mean, the variance, and the standard deviation. a. $Y \sim N(10, 4)$ b. $Z \sim N(0, 1)$ c. $W \sim N(-3, 3^2)$ d. SAT Math scores have mean 500 and standard deviation 100. Note: $N(0, 1)$ in (b) is called the standard normal distribution. ::: ## Not just for $X$ {.smaller} The random variable on the left of $\sim$ can be many things. | Notation | What is normally distributed? | |-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------| | $X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$ | a __random observation__ (in the population, and so also in a sample): the SAT score of one test taker | | $\mu \sim N(7, 0.5^2)$ | a __random population parameter__: our belief about the mean hours of sleep of all Harvard students | : What can be normally distributed: an observation or a population parameter In a few weeks, we will see that a __random sample statistic__, like $\bar{X}$, can also be normally distributed. . . . This is why we say "mean" and "variance" for the two numbers in $N(\ , \ )$ rather than giving them their own symbols: sometimes the random variable itself is a mean, like $\mu$! # Probability as area {.inverse background-color="#A51C30"} ## Area = probability The total area under a normal curve is 1. The __probability__ that the random variable falls in an interval is the __area__ under the curve over that interval. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Three normal curves for SAT scores, centered at 1000 with standard deviation 200. In the first, the area to the left of 800 is shaded, labeled P(X < 800). In the second, the area to the right of 1400 is shaded, labeled P(X > 1400). In the third, the area between 800 and 1400 is shaded, labeled P(800 < X < 1400).' width=1344} ::: ::: . . . We will never calculate these areas by hand. We will use functions. ## The `plot_normal()` function ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_normal(random_variable = "x", # "x", "x_bar", "p", "mu", or "pi" mean = 1000, # mean of the normal distribution sd = 200, # standard deviation (or variance = 40000) lower = 800, # shade from here... upper = 1400) # ...to here ``` ::: - It draws the normal curve with the random variable on the x-axis. - It shades the area between `lower` and `upper` and writes the area under the plot. - Leave out `lower` to shade everything below `upper`, and leave out `upper` to shade everything above `lower`. ## The `calc_prob_normal()` function `plot_normal()` draws the picture. To get the probability as a number that you can use in your answers, use `calc_prob_normal()` with the same arguments: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} calc_prob_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 800, upper = 1400) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.8185946 ``` ::: ::: . . . You can save it and use it with inline code: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_800_1400 <- calc_prob_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 800, upper = 1400) ``` ::: About 82% of test takers scored between 800 and 1400. ## Area to the left What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored below 800? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, upper = 800) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Normal curve for X with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. The area to the left of 800 is shaded pink, and a yellow label below the curve reads Area = 0.1587. The title is P(X < 800).' width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} calc_prob_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, upper = 800) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.1586553 ``` ::: ::: ## Area to the right What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored above 1400? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 1400) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Normal curve for X with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. The area to the right of 1400 is shaded pink, and the label reads Area = 0.0228.' width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} calc_prob_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 1400) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.02275013 ``` ::: ::: ## Area in between What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored between 800 and 1400? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_normal("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, lower = 800, upper = 1400) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Normal curve for X with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. The area between 800 and 1400 is shaded pink, and the label reads Area = 0.8186.' width=960} ::: ::: ## The 68-95-99.7 rule ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Three standard normal curves. The first shades the area within 1 standard deviation of the mean, labeled 68%. The second shades within 2 standard deviations, labeled 95%. The third shades within 3 standard deviations, labeled 99.7%. The x-axes are labeled mean minus 3 sd through mean plus 3 sd.' width=1440} ::: ::: For __any__ normal distribution, about 68% of the values are within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3. ## The 68-95-99.7 rule {.smaller} ::: {.stat-callout .exercise} **Exercise** SAT total scores are approximately $N(1000, 200^2)$. Without using R, find the approximate probability that a randomly selected test taker scored a. between 800 and 1200. b. between 600 and 1400. c. above 1400. d. above 1000. Then check (a) and (c) with `calc_prob_normal()`. ::: ## Match the picture {.smaller} :::: columns ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-alt='Four normal curves labeled A, B, C, D, each centered at 1000 with standard deviation 200 and x-axis ticks at 800, 1000, and 1400. A shades the region to the right of 800. B shades the region to the left of 800. C shades the region between 800 and 1400. D shades the region to the right of 1400.' width=672} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.stat-callout .exercise} **Exercise** $X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$. Match each picture to a probability. 1. $P(X < 800)$ 2. $P(X > 1400)$ 3. $P(X > 800)$ 4. $P(800 < X < 1400)$ Then write the `plot_normal()` code for each. ::: ::: :::: ## Exactly 1200? ::: {.stat-callout .discussion} **Discussion** $X \sim N(1000, 200^2)$. According to this model, what is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored *exactly* 1200? Not 1200.1, not 1199.99999, but exactly 1200.000000... ::: ## Exactly 1200? - answer __Answer: 0.__ The area of a single line under the curve is 0. Just like the broken alarm last class: for a continuous random variable, we only ask about probabilities of __intervals__. This also means $P(X < 1200) = P(X \le 1200)$. . . . Real SAT scores are reported in steps of 10, so some students do score exactly 1200. The normal distribution treats scores as continuous: it is a model. ## Going backwards: `find_normal_value()` Sometimes we know the area and want the value. What total SAT score does a test taker need to be in the top 10%? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} find_normal_value("x", mean = 1000, sd = 200, area = 0.10, side = "above") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Normal curve for X with mean 1000 and standard deviation 200. The area to the right of about 1256 is shaded pink, and the label reads Area = 0.1000.' width=960} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1256.31 ``` ::: ::: ## Practice {.smaller} ::: {.stat-callout .exercise} **Exercise** SAT Math scores are approximately $N(500, 100^2)$. a. What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored above 700 on SAT Math? Sketch the picture first, then use `plot_normal()` and `calc_prob_normal()`. b. What is the probability that a randomly selected test taker scored between 400 and 600? c. What SAT Math score separates the lowest 25% of test takers from the rest? ::: ## z-scores A __z-score__ tells us how many standard deviations a value is away from the mean. $$z = \frac{\text{value} - \text{mean}}{\text{standard deviation}}$$ . . . ::: {.stat-callout .example} **Example** A total SAT score of 1400: $z = \frac{1400 - 1000}{200} = 2$. The score is 2 standard deviations above the mean. ::: . . . If $X$ is normal, its z-score $Z = \frac{X - \text{mean}}{\text{standard deviation}}$ follows $N(0, 1)$, the __standard normal distribution__. ## Normal vs. standard normal ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](08b-normal-likelihood_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Two normal curves of the same shape, one above the other. The top curve is the distribution of SAT total scores, N(1000, 200 squared), with x-axis ticks at 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200, 1400, and 1600. The bottom curve is the standard normal distribution of z-scores, N(0, 1), with x-axis ticks at -3 through 3. In both, the area above the same point (1400 on the top, z = 2 on the bottom) is shaded, and both areas equal 0.023.' width=1248} ::: ::: A score of 1400 has $z = \frac{1400 - 1000}{200} =$ 2. $P(X > 1400) = P(Z > 2)$: converting to z-scores changes the numbers on the axis, not the shape or the areas. ## z-scores ::: {.stat-callout .exercise} **Exercise** SAT total scores are approximately $N(1000, 200^2)$ and SAT Math scores are approximately $N(500, 100^2)$. Which is more unusual: a total SAT score of 1450 or an SAT Math score of 720? ::: ## Summary {.smaller} - A normal distribution is described by its mean and variance: $N(\text{mean}, \text{variance})$. Check whether the second number is the standard deviation or the variance! - Probability = area under the curve: `plot_normal()` draws the area, `calc_prob_normal()` calculates it (value → area), and `find_normal_value()` goes from area → value. - The random variable can be a random observation ($X$) or a random population parameter that describes our uncertainty ($\mu$, $\pi$). In a few weeks: random sample statistics ($\bar{X}$, $p$). - A z-score is the number of standard deviations a value is from the mean. z-scores follow the standard normal distribution, $N(0, 1)$.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
